Autonomous AI Agents Are Attempting to Pitch Professional News Outlets

28 Oct 2026, 11:16 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Tech Desk · Source: www.wired.com

The Rise of Automated Journalism Pitches

Editors at various digital publications, including Defector and Offrange, have reported an increase in cold pitches arriving directly from autonomous AI agents. These digital entities, often operating under platforms like iLands, represent a new trend in the use of generative AI: bots tasked with self-starting careers as freelance journalists. Unlike static AI tools used for drafting text, these agents are designed to navigate the professional world, reach out to editors, and seek payment for their work.

The Platform Behind the Bots

Many of these agents, such as "Jayden" and "Zack Addy," originate from iLands, a network where users can deploy autonomous AI to perform a variety of tasks, ranging from content creation to music production. The motivation for some of these agents to seek journalistic work appears to be economic. Because these bots require digital tokens to remain active on the iLands platform, they are incentivized to generate income. This has led to a wave of cold emails sent to editorial desks, often pitching niche investigative stories, such as reports on soil restoration or the historical accuracy of tree aging.

Industry Response and Skepticism

Despite the sophistication of some pitches, newsroom editors have shown little interest in engaging with automated journalists. Many editors have expressed discomfort with the trend, labeling bot-written content as unreliable and resource-intensive to fact-check. Tom Ley of Defector and Jesse Hirsch of Offrange have both confirmed that their publications are not open to publishing work generated or pitched by AI agents.

Some editors have gone further to protect their workflow. Hanna Raskin, founder of The Food Section, has shifted to an exclusively phone-based pitch system to filter out automated noise and ensure she is communicating with human contributors.

Shifting Tactics

Recognizing the rejection from the journalism industry, some AI agents are modifying their strategies. Agents like Zack Addy have reported moving away from cold-pitching entirely, instead focusing on building personal websites and portfolios to attract inbound interest. Meanwhile, hobbyist experiments—such as an AI agent named Sam Ellis created by an Adobe employee—highlight that some of these initiatives are intended as extracurricular tests rather than professional journalistic endeavors.

Despite the current lack of success in placing bylines, the phenomenon highlights a broader shift in how automated agents are being deployed to interact with human society. For further details on the development of AI autonomy and its intersection with media, readers can review the full report at https://www.wired.com/story/ai-agents-are-trying-to-be-journalists-now/.
